This vignette serves as a diagnostic for the second model, which examines the relationship between species’ phenological sensitivity and climatic mismatch between their native niches and the urban climatic context. I first describe the definition of climatic safety margins and compare this model with alternative specifications that rely solely on urban climatic context.

## Prepare species-city model coefficients

```{r input}

### Group by city and phe_type
tree_dir <- "~/lab-data/datasets/vegetation/StreetTrees/cleaned_ps_input/"
rds_files <- list.files(tree_dir, pattern = "\\.rds$", full.names = TRUE)
cities <- gsub("\\.rds$", "", basename(rds_files))
phe_types <- c("SOS", "EOS")

coef_summary_all <- data.frame()

for (city in cities) {
  r_output_dir <- paste0("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/model_output/final_models_clean_outlier/inla/spatial_spde/", city, "/canonicalname/")
  for (phe_type in phe_types) {
    file_path <- file.path(r_output_dir, paste0(phe_type, "_summary.rds"))
    if (file.exists(file_path)) {
      coef_summary <- readr::read_rds(file_path) |>
        dplyr::mutate(phe_type = phe_type, city = city)
      coef_summary_all <- dplyr::bind_rows(coef_summary_all, coef_summary)
    }
  }
}
coef_summary_all <- coef_summary_all |>
  mutate(phe_type = factor(phe_type, levels = c("SOS", "EOS")),
         genus = sub(" .*", "", Factor),
         species = Factor) |>
  left_join(
    readr::read_rds("~/phenology-urban/temp/tree_genus_family.rds"),
    by = "genus")

inventory_centroids <- readRDS(("~/lab-data/datasets/vegetation/StreetTrees/cleaned_ps_input/summary/inventory_centroids.rds"))
boundary_us <- st_read(("~/lab-data/datasets/boundary/USAdministrative/US/us_boundarydissolve.shp"), quiet = T) |>
  st_transform(4326)

load("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/model_output/final_models_clean_outlier/inla/spatial_spde/tree_species.RData") # phylo_tree

load("~/phenology-urban/temp/tree_family.RData") # tree_family

city_feature <- readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/raw/CONUS/StreetTrees/cleaned_ps_input/summary/city_bioclimate.rds") |>
  select(site, bio1, bio12) |>

```

## Calculate speices climate mismatch

To further examine whether species’ climatic origins influence their phenological sensitivity in urban environments, I will assess whether species originating from warmer or colder climates exhibit systematically different phenological responses to urban temperature variation. Using the species list, I will first extract global occurrence records from GBIF to characterize each species’ native climatic niche. Following a safety-margin framework, I will then quantify the climatic mismatch between species’ native conditions and the urban environments in which they occur.

Specifically, I introduce the concept of "safety margin". The safety margin was used initially in the field of plant hydraulics to describe the difference between the level of water stress experienced by a species in the field and the level of water stress leading to hydraulic failure. Extending this concept to the context of climatic niches, I calculate two types of safety margins for each species in each city:

- **Hot edge safety margin**: $$S_{\mathrm{bio1},m,n}
= \mathrm{bio1}_n - Q_{0.95}\!\left(\mathrm{bio1}_m\right)$$ where $\mathrm{bio1}_n$ is the mean annual temperature of the city $n$, and $Q_{0.95}\!\left(\mathrm{bio1}_m\right)$ is the 95th percentile of mean annual temperature across the species $m$’ native range. 

- **Dry edge safety margin**: $$S_{\mathrm{bio12},m,n}
= \mathrm{bio12}_n - Q_{0.05}\!\left(\mathrm{bio12}_m\right)$$ where $\mathrm{bio12}_n$ is the annual precipitation of the city $n$, and $Q_{0.05}\!\left(\mathrm{bio12}_m\right)$ is the 5th percentile of annual precipitation across the species $m$’ native range.

>| There is something I am still struggling with. I want to focus on one-sided mismatches for the hot edge and the dry edge. Under our current definition, positive values of $S_{\mathrm{bio1}}$ indicate thermal mismatch, with larger values corresponding to stronger mismatch, whereas for $S_{\mathrm{bio12}}$, negative values indicate mismatch, with more negative values representing stronger drought-related mismatch. Although the directions of the two metrics are opposite, this setup is intuitive given the meanings of temperature and precipitation extremes (hotter means higher value vs. drier means lower value). In another [study](https://www-nature-com.proxy.lib.umich.edu/articles/s41558-022-01465-8#Sec6), the positions of city-level and species-level values for $\mathrm{bio1}$ are reversed, such that negative values ($S < 0$) uniformly indicate that a species is already experiencing "unsafe" climatic conditions under the baseline, with more negative values corresponding to stronger mismatch.

```{r gbif-occurrence}
city_inven_backbone <- read_rds("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/model_output/final_models_clean_outlier/inla/spatial_spde/city_inven_backbone.rds")

city_inven_backbone_filtered <- city_inven_backbone |>
  filter(
    kingdom == "Plantae", phylum == "Tracheophyta",
    rank %in% c("GENUS", "SPECIES"),
    status %in% c("ACCEPTED", "SYNONYM")
  )

city_inven_backbone_filtered_consolidated <- city_inven_backbone_filtered |>
  mutate(usageKey = if_else(status == "SYNONYM", acceptedUsageKey, usageKey))
```

```{r summarize-range}
overlap_city_species_range <- coef_summary_all |>
  left_join(city_inven_backbone_filtered_consolidated |>
              select(usageKey, verbatim_name), by = c("Factor" = "verbatim_name")) |>
  left_join(read_rds("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/tree_origin/chelsa/sp_chelsa_summary.rds"),
            by = c("usageKey" = "specieskey")) |>

              mutate(city = ifelse(city == "St_George", "StGeorge", city)) |>
              mutate(city = ifelse(city == "St.Louis", "StLouis", city)) |>              
              st_drop_geometry(), by = "city")
```

## Model fitting

### Current version (Safety margin only)

```{r}
overlap_city_species_range_model <- overlap_city_species_range |>
  mutate(hot_edge = bio1 - bio1_p95,
         cold_edge = bio1_p5 - bio1,
         d_temp = bio1 - bio1_median,
         d_prcp = bio12 - bio12_median,
         temp_breadth = bio1_p95 - bio1_p5,
         prcp_breadth = bio12_p95 - bio12_p5,
         dry_edge = bio12 - bio12_p5)  |>
  select(-bio1, -bio12, -species)# larger value: further away from the edge 
```

#### Univariate model for single species (for visualization)

I fit univariate models for each species separately to visualize the relationship between phenological sensitivity and safety margin for each species:

$$y_{m,n} = \theta_{0,m} + \theta_{1,m}\, S_{\mathrm{bio12},m,n} + \varepsilon_{m,n}$$

or

$$y_{m,n} = \theta_{0,m} + \theta_{1,m}\, S_{\mathrm{bio1},m,n} + \varepsilon_{m,n}$$

$$\varepsilon_{m,n} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\; \frac{\sigma_m^2}{w_{m,n}}\right)$$

where $y_{m,n}$ is the estimated phenological sensitivity (temperature coefficient) for species $m$ in city $n$, $\theta_{0,m}$ is the species-specific intercept, $\theta_{1,m}$ is the species-specific slope representing the relationship between phenological sensitivity and safety margin, and $\varepsilon_{m,n}$ is the error term with variance inversely proportional to the weights $w_{m,n}$. Weights were defined as the inverse of the posterior variance of the estimated temperature sensitivity, i.e., $w_{m,n} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{SD}_{m,n}^2}$, where $\mathrm{SD}_{m,n}$ is the posterior standard deviation associated with $y_{m,n}$.


#### Multivariate model for all species (for inference)

Here is the model I used in the manuscript, with the safety margin defined as above.

$$y_{m,n} = \mathbf{z}_{m, n} \boldsymbol{\lambda} +b_{m} + \epsilon_{m,n}$$

$$\mathbf{z}_{m,n} = [1, S_{\mathrm{bio1},m,n}, S_{\mathrm{bio12},m,n}]$$

$$\boldsymbol{\lambda} = (\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2)^\top$$

$$\boldsymbol{\lambda} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbf{0}, \sigma_\lambda^2 \mathbf{I}\right)$$

$$\mathbf{b} = (b_1, \dots, b_M)^\top \sim \mathcal{MVN}\!\left(\mathbf{0},\; \sigma^2_{\mathrm{phy}}\,\mathbf{A}\right)$$

$$\epsilon_{m,n} \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2_\varepsilon)$$

where $y_{m,n}$ is the estimated phenological sensitivity for species $m$ in city $n$, $\mathbf{z}_{m,n}$ is the vector of predictors including the intercept and the safety margins for temperature and precipitation, $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ is the vector of fixed effects, $b_m$ is the random effect for species $m$ accounting for phylogenetic relatedness with covariance matrix $\mathbf{A}$, and $\epsilon_{m,n}$ is the residual error term.

#### Univariate model for single species (for visualization)

For visualization, replacing the climatic safety margin with the city’s bioclimatic context is mathematically equivalent to subtracting a species-specific constant, effectively shifting points along the x-axis. As a result, this transformation preserves the underlying relationship observed in the original analysis.

I personally prefer the safety-margin version, as framing the analysis in terms of climatic distance may provide additional biological insight by explicitly capturing the degree of mismatch between a species’ native climatic range and the urban environment.

#### Multivariate model for all species (for inference)

Here is the model replacing safety margin with bioclimatic condition ($\mathrm{bio1}_n, \mathrm{bio12}_n$) for city $n$:

$$y_{m,n} = \mathbf{z}_{m, n} \boldsymbol{\lambda} +b_{m} + \epsilon_{m,n}$$

$$\mathbf{z}_{m,n} = [1, \mathrm{bio1}_n, \mathrm{bio12}_n]$$

$$\boldsymbol{\lambda} = (\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2)^\top$$

Because the combination of bootstrapping and `phyr` is computationally intensive, I initially fitted the model using `brms` with point estimates.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
m_SOS <- fit_multi_pglmm(phe_type = "SOS", input_data = overlap_city_species_range_model, city_feature, package = "phyr", prcp = "bio12", temp = "bio1", bootstrap = T)
m_EOS <- fit_multi_pglmm(phe_type = "EOS", input_data = overlap_city_species_range_model, city_feature, package = "phyr", prcp = "bio12", temp = "bio1", bootstrap = T)

model_list_multi <- list(m_SOS, m_EOS)
write_rds(model_list_multi, "~/phenology-urban/data/proc/model_output/final_models_clean_outlier/inla/model_multi_bioclimate_phylo_test.rds")

model_list_multi <- read_rds("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/model_output/final_models_clean_outlier/freq/model_multi_bioclimate.rds")
```

```{r fig-multivariate-bioclimate}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
#| message: false
m_SOS$plot + m_EOS$plot
```

Compared with the previous model, the directions of the effects remain consistent, except that the precipitation effect on the SOS response becomes non-significant.

### Distance from niche centroid

```{r}
overlap_city_species_range_model <- overlap_city_species_range |>
  mutate(hot_edge = bio1 - bio1_p95,
         cold_edge = bio1_p5 - bio1,
         d_temp = bio1 - bio1_median,
         d_prcp = bio12 - bio12_median,
         temp_breadth = bio1_p95 - bio1_p5,
         prcp_breadth = bio12_p95 - bio12_p5,
         dry_edge = bio12 - bio12_p5)  |>
  select(-bio1, -bio12, -species)# larger value: further away from the edge 

source("~/phenology-urban/script/fit_pglmm_model.R")
load("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/model_output/final_models_clean_outlier/inla/spatial_spde/tree_species.RData")
```

#### Univariate model for single species (for visualization)

For visualization, replacing the climatic safety margin with the deviation of climatic context from species' niche centroid is still mathematically equivalent to subtracting a species-specific constant, effectively shifting points along the x-axis.

```{r fig-univariate-centroid}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5

clim = "d_prcp"
phe_type = "EOS"
x_lab <- if (rlang::as_name(clim) %in% c("bio1")) {
  expression("Mean annual temperature ("*degree*C*")")
} else if (rlang::as_name(clim) %in% c("bio12")) {
  "Mean annual precipitation (mm)"
} else {
  rlang::as_name(clim)
}

pred_df <- lapply(
  species_vec,
  function(sp) {
    fit_uni(
      phe_type = phe_type, input_data = overlap_city_species_range_model, city_feature = city_feature, species_name = sp, clim = clim, bootstrap = T)$pred_table
  }
) |>
  bind_rows()

fit_input_df <- overlap_city_species_range_model |>
  left_join(city_feature, by = "city") |>
  filter(Factor %in% species_vec, phe_type == !!phe_type) |>
  select(Estimate, Lower, Upper, !!clim, Factor)
x_vals <- fit_input_df[[clim]]
x_min  <- min(x_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
x_max  <- max(x_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
x_rng  <- x_max - x_min

p_EOS <- ggplot(fit_input_df, aes(x = .data[[clim]], y = Estimate, color = Factor)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper), alpha = 0.1, size = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(data = pred_df,
              aes(x = .data[[clim]], ymin = y_lwr, ymax = y_upr, fill = species),
              inherit.aes = FALSE,
              alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = pred_df,
            aes(x = .data[[clim]], y = y_pred, color = species),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            linewidth = 0.5) +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(x_min - 0.15 * x_rng, x_max)
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    x = x_lab,
    y = paste0("Estimated effect on ", phe_type),
    color = "Species",
    fill  = "Species"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.text = element_text(face = "italic")
    # axis.title = element_blank()
  )

clim = "d_temp"
phe_type = "SOS"
x_lab <- if (rlang::as_name(clim) %in% c("bio1")) {
  expression("Mean annual temperature ("*degree*C*")")
} else if (rlang::as_name(clim) %in% c("bio12")) {
  "Mean annual precipitation (mm)"
} else {

}

) |>
```

#### Multivariate model for all species (for inference)

Here is the model replacing safety margin with deviation of climatic contexts from species' niche centroids:

$$y_{m,n} = \mathbf{z}_{m, n} \boldsymbol{\lambda} +b_{m} + \epsilon_{m,n}$$

$$\mathbf{z}_{m,n} = [1, (\mathrm{bio1}_n - Q_{0.50}\!\left(\mathrm{bio1}_m\right)), (\mathrm{bio12}_n - Q_{0.50}\!\left(\mathrm{bio12}_m\right))]$$

$$\boldsymbol{\lambda} = (\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2)^\top$$

Because the combination of bootstrapping and `phyr` is computationally intensive, I initially fitted the model using `brms` with point estimates.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
m_SOS <- fit_multi_pglmm("SOS", overlap_city_species_range_model, city_feature, package = "brms", prcp = "d_prcp", temp = "d_temp")
m_EOS <- fit_multi_pglmm("EOS", overlap_city_species_range_model, city_feature, package = "brms", prcp = "d_prcp", temp = "d_temp")
```

```{r fig-multivariate-centroid}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
#| message: false
m_SOS$plot + m_EOS$plot
```

I think this conveys information consistent with the "safety margin" version; the main difference is which framing is more ecologically interpretable.

```{r eval=FALSE}
m_SOS <- fit_multi_pglmm("SOS", overlap_city_species_range_model, city_feature, package = "phyr", prcp = "bio12", temp = "bio1", bootstrap = T)
m_EOS <- fit_multi_pglmm("EOS", overlap_city_species_range_model, city_feature, package = "phyr", prcp = "bio12", temp = "bio1", bootstrap = T)

model_list_multi <- list(m_SOS, m_EOS)
write_rds(model_list_multi, "~/phenology-urban/data/proc/model_output/final_models_clean_outlier/inla/model_multi_bioclimate.rds")
```
